These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes.

changed_units.before: Three assumptions have different jobs. [**Stationarity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that moving the observation window does not change the map's probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation. It does not say that a particular map is flat. [**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$. It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy. Finally, smoothness controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives. Crossing calculations below require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation. A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below.
changed_units.after:
Three assumptions have different jobs:

- [**Stationarity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that moving the observation window does not change the map's probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation. It does not say that a particular map is flat.
- [**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$. It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy.
- [**Smoothness**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives. Crossing calculations require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation.

A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below.
changed_units.correctness_evidence: The list retains separate stationarity and isotropy requirements, differentiable samples, invertible derivative covariance, stronger second-derivative requirements for peaks, and the nondifferentiable exponential-covariance counterexample. No assumption becomes an implication of Gaussian marginal values.

changed_units.before: Finding every root of a random curve is difficult. Counting how often the curve passes a level is easier because a small interval around a crossing has a width determined by its slope.
changed_units.after: A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope; this lets us count crossings without locating every root.
changed_units.correctness_evidence: The revised transition connects the field-count question to the slope-weighted crossing identity. The next narrow-band calculation retains a simple upward crossing, positive slope and regularity; the finite-track endpoint contribution remains explicit later.

changed_units.before: The [**Euler characteristic**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, written $\chi$, combines these counts. In 1D it equals the number of connected active intervals. In 2D it is the number of connected components minus the number of independent holes. Three disjoint disks have $\chi=3$; one connected ring has $\chi=1-1=0$. In 3D it is components minus independent tunnels plus enclosed cavities. A solid ball has $\chi=1$, a solid ring has $\chi=0$, and a hollow spherical shell has $\chi=2$. These counts are the first three [**Betti numbers**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: numbers of independent components, loops, and cavities, respectively.[^p3-ec-source]
changed_units.after:
The [**Euler characteristic**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, written $\chi$, combines these counts differently in each dimension:

- In 1D it equals the number of connected active intervals.
- In 2D it is the number of connected components minus the number of independent holes. Three disjoint disks have $\chi=3$; one connected ring has $\chi=1-1=0$.
- In 3D it is components minus independent tunnels plus enclosed cavities. A solid ball has $\chi=1$, a solid ring has $\chi=0$, and a hollow spherical shell has $\chi=2$.

These counts are the first three [**Betti numbers**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: numbers of independent components, loops, and cavities, respectively.[^p3-ec-source]
changed_units.correctness_evidence: The dimensional Euler-characteristic rules and all examples are unchanged. The signs agree with beta0 minus beta1 plus beta2: disk components, ring, solid torus and shell are distinguished from positive field counts.

changed_units.before: The expected Euler characteristic has an exact Gaussian formula even where identifying it with field count would be wrong. We already derived the 1D case. To understand the higher dimensional factors, we use a mathematical input: for a smooth function on a compact domain whose critical points have zero gradient and invertible Hessians, the Euler characteristic of a level set region can be computed as a signed count of critical points, including boundary contributions. This is the relevant conclusion of Morse theory. We do not prove that topological theorem here. The calculation below shows how its Gaussian expectation produces the paper's polynomials and boundary terms; the general Gaussian result is given by Taylor's kinematic formula.[^p3-taylor]

changed_units.before: The limiting checks are informative. As $q\to-\infty$, the whole box becomes active and all three expectations tend to one. As $q\to+\infty$, they tend to zero. At intermediate thresholds the higher dimensional signed densities can be negative because tunnels or holes outnumber components. For example a cube with $L/\sigma=10$ has expected $\chi=-20.06$ at $q=0$. A negative expected Euler characteristic is meaningful; a negative expected field count would not be.
changed_units.after:
The formulas have two limiting checks:

- As $q\to-\infty$, the whole box becomes active and all three expectations tend to one.
- As $q\to+\infty$, they tend to zero.

At intermediate thresholds the higher dimensional signed densities can be negative because tunnels or holes outnumber components. For example a cube with $L/\sigma=10$ has expected $\chi=-20.06$ at $q=0$. A negative expected Euler characteristic is meaningful; a negative expected field count would not be.
changed_units.correctness_evidence: The two threshold limits are separate checks of the same bounded closed box: full occupancy gives Euler characteristic one and empty occupancy gives zero. Negative intermediate Euler characteristic remains distinguished from an impossible negative component count.

changed_units.before:
The processing choices affect the quantities being compared. Bat maps were rectified at about 0.5 Hz for denoising. The 3D maps, sampled in 10 cm bins, also received a median filter. Fields larger than three standard deviations above mean 3D volume were removed as possible merges, including from slice analyses. Peak counting excluded incomplete boundary fields and used a range of smoothing widths. The 1D rate versus width comparison used an additional 1 Hz cutoff. These decisions can remove small components, alter peaks, and change tails. They belong to the definition of the analyzed fields.[^p3-processing]

The supplement adds useful checks. Figure S1 matches the rat maze's 15 cm minimum length cutoff in simulations and removes unusually large empirical fields; changing that cutoff changes log-length moments. Figure S5 shows sensitivity of the higher-moment comparison across small denoising thresholds, while the rate versus width slope becomes stable above about 1 Hz. Figure S2 compares the spherical-field alternative and measures boundary curvature. Locally, mean curvature averages bending in two principal directions and Gaussian curvature multiplies them: a spherical patch bends the same way in both directions, while a saddle bends in opposite directions. These are extra shape measurements; they are not needed to derive the field-size law. Surface representations and finite differences affect their estimates.[^p3-supp-tests]

- Peak counting excluded incomplete boundary fields and used a range of smoothing widths.
- The 1D rate versus width comparison used an additional 1 Hz cutoff.

These decisions can remove small components, alter peaks, and change tails. They belong to the definition of the analyzed fields.[^p3-processing]
